question: What are the two primary and essentially distinct functions of an modern operating system?
options: A. Compiling programs and managing networks
B. Providing an extended machine (abstractions) and managing hardware resources
C. Executing user applications and securing database servers
D. Managing web interfaces and formatting storage drives
explanation: An operating system performs two primary functions: acting as an extended machine that provides clean abstractions to application programs, and acting as a resource manager that allocates hardware resources [1, 2].

question: In the concept of the operating system as an extended machine, what is its primary purpose?
options: A. To hide the messy hardware details and present user programs with a simpler, cleaner virtual machine
B. To speed up arithmetic calculations on the CPU
C. To prevent application programmers from accessing high-level languages
D. To directly expose disk controller registers to application programs
explanation: As an extended machine, the OS hides the complex and awkward hardware details (such as disk controllers) and presents a simpler virtual machine interface [1, 3, 4].

question: Which of the following describes resource multiplexing in time?
options: A. Dividing main memory among different active programs simultaneously
B. Partitioning a hard disk into multiple tracks and sectors
C. Programs or users taking turns sequentially using a single CPU
D. Assigning dedicated CPU cores to specific threads permanently
explanation: When a resource is time-multiplexed, different programs or users take turns using it, such as multiple processes sharing a single CPU sequentially [1, 5].

question: Which mode of CPU execution gives the operating system full access to all hardware and all machine instructions?
options: A. User mode
B. Kernel mode (Supervisor mode)
C. Protected application mode
D. Safe mode
explanation: In kernel mode (also called supervisor mode), the CPU has complete access to all hardware and can execute any instruction the machine is capable of executing [6-8].

question: Why are certain instructions (such as I/O instructions) disallowed in user mode?
options: A. To reduce power consumption of the processor
B. Because user-mode programs do not have enough memory to run them
C. To prevent user programs from interfering with the system or gaining unauthorized hardware control
D. Because user programs only run in assembly language
explanation: Instructions that control machine hardware or perform I/O are forbidden in user mode to prevent user processes from compromising system stability and security [8, 9].

question: What major hardware technology characterized the First Generation (1945–1955) of computers?
options: A. Vacuum tubes and plugboards
B. Transistors
C. Integrated circuits (ICs)
D. VLSI microprocessors
explanation: The first generation of computers used vacuum tubes and plugboards, operated without any operating system, and relied on absolute machine language [1, 10, 11].

question: During the Second Generation (1955–1965), which type of system was introduced to reduce wasted computer setup time?
options: A. Real-time distributed systems
B. Batch systems
C. Interactive graphical systems
D. Client-server systems
explanation: Second-generation computers introduced batch systems to collect a tray of jobs on cards, transfer them to magnetic tape, and process them sequentially to minimize idle time [1, 10, 12].

question: In early batch systems using the IBM 1401 and IBM 7094, what was the primary role of the IBM 1401?
options: A. Performing high-speed numerical calculations
B. Reading cards onto tape and printing output off-line
C. Compiling complex FORTRAN programs
D. Managing multi-user timesharing networks
explanation: The less expensive IBM 1401 was used to read punched cards onto magnetic tape and print output off-line, leaving the expensive IBM 7094 to do the actual computing [12-14].

question: What key technique popularized in the Third Generation (1965–1980) kept the CPU busy while a job was waiting for I/O?
options: A. Spooling only
B. Multiprogramming
C. Monoprogramming
D. Virtual reality processing
explanation: Multiprogramming keeps multiple jobs in memory simultaneously so that when one job blocks waiting for I/O, the CPU can switch to another job [1, 15].

question: What was the first general-purpose timesharing system, developed at M.I.T. on a modified IBM 7094?
options: B. MULTICS
C. CTSS (Compatible Time Sharing System)
D. MINIX
explanation: CTSS (Compatible Time Sharing System) was developed at M.I.T. on a specially modified IBM 7094 as the first general-purpose timesharing system [16].

question: Which operating system envisioned computing as a public utility like electricity and introduced concentric protection rings?
options: A. MS-DOS
B. MULTICS
C. CP/M
D. FMS
explanation: MULTICS (Multiplexed Information and Computing Service) was designed as a massive computing utility and introduced concentric rings of protection [17, 18].

question: Which operating system category is characterized by having time as the absolute key parameter and meeting strict deadlines?
options: A. Real-time operating systems
B. Batch processing systems
C. Personal computer operating systems
D. Mainframe transaction systems
explanation: Real-time operating systems are characterized by having time as a critical parameter; they must deliver correct responses within specified deadlines [19, 20].

question: What distinguishes a 'hard' real-time system from a 'soft' real-time system?
options: A. Hard real-time systems run only on mainframes, while soft real-time runs on PCs
B. Missing an absolute deadline in a hard real-time system causes catastrophic failure, whereas in soft real-time it is tolerable
C. Hard real-time systems do not use interrupts
D. Soft real-time systems do not require clocks or timers
explanation: In hard real-time systems, missing a deadline risks total system failure; in soft real-time systems, missing an occasional deadline degrades performance but does not cause permanent damage [19-22].

question: What is a defining characteristic of embedded operating systems?
options: A. They always provide multi-window GUIs for end users
B. They run in devices not thought of as computers and do not accept untrusted user-installed software
C. They require gigabytes of disk storage to operate
D. They are designed exclusively for banking mainframe transactions
explanation: Embedded systems run in devices like microwave ovens, TVs, and cars where software is stored in ROM and untrusted user-installed software is not permitted [23, 24].

question: Which type of operating system runs on small chips with severe processing power and memory constraints, such as for electronic payments?
options: A. Server operating systems
B. Smart card operating systems
C. Personal computer operating systems
D. Mainframe operating systems
explanation: Smart card operating systems run on CPU chips embedded in cards with severe memory and CPU constraints, handling specific operations like electronic payments [23, 25].

question: Which CPU register contains the condition bits, CPU priority, and the current execution mode (user or kernel mode)?
options: A. Program Counter (PC)
B. Stack Pointer (SP)
C. Program Status Word (PSW)
D. Memory Address Register (MAR)
explanation: The Program Status Word (PSW) contains condition code bits, CPU priority, mode bits (user/kernel), and other control information [9, 26].

question: How do base and limit registers protect memory in a multiprogrammed system?
options: A. By encrypting all data written to the hard drive
B. By checking every memory reference against the limit register and adding the base register to physical addresses
C. By preventing user programs from executing arithmetic operations
D. By swapping user programs to magnetic tape automatically
explanation: The CPU automatically adds the base register to generated addresses and ensures the address does not exceed the limit register; references outside this range trigger a trap [27-30].

question: What is a 'trap' instruction in computer architecture?
options: A. An asynchronous hardware signal sent by an external device
B. A software-generated interrupt that switches CPU execution from user mode to kernel mode
C. A hardware fault caused by a broken electrical circuit
D. An instruction that stops CPU clock cycles permanently
explanation: A trap is a software-generated interrupt caused by a user request (such as a system call) or an exceptional condition (like divide by zero) that transfers control to the OS in kernel mode [6, 9, 31, 32].

question: What is the function of the interrupt vector in an operating system?
options: A. An array that lists all currently open file names
B. A table of memory addresses pointing to the respective interrupt service procedures
C. A queue that stores pending user batch jobs
D. A hardware register that counts the number of instructions executed
explanation: The interrupt vector is an area in memory containing the starting addresses of the service routines (handlers) for each class of interrupt or device [26, 31, 33].

question: What is the primary drawback of programmed I/O (polling/busy waiting)?
options: A. It requires complex interrupt controller hardware
B. The CPU wastes substantial time in a tight loop repeatedly polling the device status
C. It cannot transfer data to character devices
D. It can only be executed in user mode
explanation: In programmed I/O, the CPU constantly polls the device to see if it is ready, which ties up the processor in a busy-waiting loop and wastes CPU cycles [34].

question: How does Direct Memory Access (DMA) improve system efficiency during I/O operations?
options: A. By allowing the CPU to completely bypass cache memory
B. By transferring an entire block of data between device controllers and memory without continuous CPU intervention
C. By eliminating the need for device drivers
D. By executing application code inside the disk controller
explanation: A DMA controller manages the transfer of data blocks directly between memory and I/O devices, interrupting the CPU only when the entire transfer is finished [34, 35].

question: In a system with memory-mapped I/O, how does the CPU communicate with device registers?
options: A. Only through dedicated IN and OUT assembly instructions
B. By reading and writing standard memory addresses mapped to device registers
C. Exclusively via network sockets
D. By sending serial pulses through the audio port
explanation: With memory-mapped I/O, device registers are mapped into the memory address space, allowing ordinary load and store instructions to read and write device registers [36-38].

question: What is the fundamental definition of a 'process' in modern operating systems?
options: A. A passive program stored on secondary storage
B. A program in execution, along with its address space and associated system resources
C. A hardware unit that decodes machine instructions
D. A collection of file directories on a disk
explanation: A process is an abstraction representing a program in execution, including its address space, registers, program counter, and resources [39-41].

question: Which of the following are the three standard logical segments comprising a process address space?
options: A. BIOS, Kernel, and Shell
B. Text (code), Data, and Stack
C. Input, Output, and Storage
D. Sectors, Tracks, and Cylinders
explanation: A process address space logically consists of a text segment (program code), a data segment (variables), and a stack (function calls and local variables) [42, 43].

question: What data structure does the operating system maintain to save the state of a suspended process?
options: A. Inode table
B. Process table (or Process Control Block - PCB)
C. Interrupt vector
D. File allocation table
explanation: The OS maintains a process table (or PCB array) where it saves the registers, program counter, memory maps, and file descriptors of each suspended process [40, 44, 45].

question: Is the user interface (the text-based shell or GUI) part of the operating system kernel?
options: A. Yes, it is always loaded in kernel mode at memory address 0
B. No, it runs in user mode and relies on system calls to get work done
C. Yes, but only in Linux systems
D. No, because it is implemented purely in hardware circuits
explanation: The shell and GUI are user-mode programs that interact with users and invoke system calls to obtain operating system services; they are not part of the kernel [7, 44, 46].

question: In POSIX/UNIX systems, which system call is used by a parent process to create an exact duplicate child process?
options: A. execve()
B. fork()
C. clone_disk()
D. waitpid()
explanation: The fork() system call creates a child process that has an address space identical to that of the parent process [47, 48].

question: Which system call replaces the current process's memory and core image with a new executable program?
options: A. execve()
B. fork()
C. exit()
D. stat()
explanation: The execve() system call replaces the calling process's entire core image (text, data, stack) with a newly loaded executable program [47, 48].

question: What is the purpose of the POSIX waitpid() system call?
options: A. To suspend a child process until the CPU finishes I/O
B. To make the calling parent process wait until a child process terminates
C. To delay CPU execution for a specific number of microseconds
D. To wait for incoming network packets on a port
explanation: The waitpid() system call suspends the parent process until a specific child process terminates and returns its exit status [47, 48].

question: Which system call allows random access to a file by repositioning the current file offset pointer?
options: A. lseek()
B. stat()
C. chmod()
D. mount()
explanation: The lseek() system call changes the position of the file read/write pointer, enabling applications to access data at arbitrary file positions [42, 47, 48].

question: In a monolithic operating system architecture, how is the kernel structured?
options: A. Divided into independent user processes communicating only via HTTP
B. As a single large binary program where all procedures run linked together in kernel mode
C. Structured as concentric hardware rings where no procedures can call each other
D. Entirely stored inside the BIOS ROM chip
explanation: In a monolithic OS, all operating system components and drivers are linked into a single large executable that runs entirely in kernel mode [49-51].

question: What is a major vulnerability or disadvantage of a monolithic operating system?
options: A. Low execution performance due to message passing
B. A bug or crash in any driver or kernel procedure can take down the entire system
C. Inability to support virtual memory or paging
D. It cannot support multiprogramming
explanation: Because everything runs in kernel space with unrestricted access, a bug in any routine (such as a third-party device driver) can crash the entire OS [51, 52].

question: In Dijkstra's THE layered operating system, what function was handled by Layer 0?
options: A. The operator console communication
B. Processor allocation and multiprogramming
C. File management and directory lookup
D. User application execution
explanation: In the THE layered system, Layer 0 handled processor allocation, switching between processes when interrupts occurred or timers expired [53-55].

question: What is the core design philosophy of a microkernel operating system?
options: A. Placing as much code as possible in kernel mode to maximize raw speed
B. Keeping only minimal mechanisms in kernel mode, while running drivers and file systems as user-mode processes
C. Merging the user GUI directly into the processor scheduler
D. Forbidding interprocess communication
explanation: Microkernels achieve modularity and reliability by running only minimal core functions in kernel mode, pushing device drivers and file systems into user space [52, 56-58].

question: How do user programs and server processes communicate in a microkernel system such as MINIX 3?
options: A. Through shared physical registers only
B. Via message passing mediated by the microkernel
C. By directly writing to each other's private stacks
D. Through hardwired mechanical relays
explanation: In microkernel architectures like MINIX 3, user processes and service modules communicate by sending and receiving structured messages [57-59].

question: In the MINIX 3 microkernel architecture, what is the role of the 'reincarnation server'?
options: A. Periodically rebooting the hardware motherboard
B. Detecting crashed or failing drivers/servers and automatically restarting them
C. Compiling C source code into machine code
D. Formatting corrupted file system partitions
explanation: The reincarnation server monitors system servers and drivers; if one crashes or behaves erroneously, it automatically replaces and restarts it without rebooting [60].

question: What is the primary difference between a Type 1 and a Type 2 hypervisor?
options: A. Type 1 hypervisors run directly on bare hardware; Type 2 hypervisors run as software on top of a host operating system
B. Type 1 hypervisors only support Linux; Type 2 only supports Windows
C. Type 1 hypervisors are implemented purely in ROM; Type 2 are cloud-based
D. Type 1 hypervisors cannot run virtual machines
explanation: Type 1 hypervisors run directly on the bare hardware like an OS, while Type 2 hypervisors run as application programs hosted on an existing OS [61].

question: How does an exokernel differ from a traditional virtual machine monitor?
options: A. An exokernel clones the entire hardware instruction set for each user
B. An exokernel partitions physical resources and assigns subsets directly to user levels without simulating full hardware abstractions
C. An exokernel prevents any guest operating systems from running
D. An exokernel cannot manage secondary disk storage
explanation: Rather than cloning virtual hardware, an exokernel partitions resources and delegates hardware slices to user-level libraries and guest systems [62].

question: According to 'Understanding Operating Systems', which subsystem manager acts like a traffic controller, managing processes through their execution states?
options: A. Memory Manager
B. Processor Manager
C. Device Manager
D. Network Manager
explanation: The Processor Manager decides how to allocate the CPU and monitors process state transitions, functioning much like a traffic controller [63, 64].

question: What four basic tasks must every subsystem manager perform in an operating system?
options: A. Compile, link, assemble, and execute code
B. Monitor resources, enforce allocation policies, allocate resources, and deallocate resources
C. Boot firmware, read sectors, seek cylinders, and format disks
D. Create users, assign passwords, encrypt files, and log off
explanation: Regardless of subsystem, each manager must monitor its resources continuously, enforce allocation policies, allocate resources when appropriate, and deallocate them when finished [63].
